name: Yusuf Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm at half four, in the yard by five. I'm a stockman at Brookfield, the co-operative dairy out past the Holloway Road roundabout, about four hundred cows plus barley and grass for silage. First milking, then scraping out the sheds, feeding, checking the calves, and the afternoon milking from three. I drove city buses for sixteen years before this, so two years in I'm still the new boy who asks the daft questions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cows more than I ever liked passengers, honestly. They're honest, you know where you are with them. What wears me out is the learning: Pete, the herd manager, can look at a heifer and know she's going to calve tonight, and I still need him to tell me. And the phone app they want us to log everything in, I won't touch it, I keep a notebook in my top pocket and Pete types it in after. He moans, but he does it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the money side look for your family?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Better than it's ever been. The co-op pays above the going rate because the union got a proper deal in, and Amina's a school nurse, steady money. When my dad died we sold his flat, so there's close to a year's bills in the bank. The mortgage on our place in Elmford has fourteen years left, and the kids, Idris is twelve and Leila's nine, they're doing fine at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in the canteen for two years: it's a fancy search engine and the bosses got excited over nothing. The cows still need milking twice a day, and no chatbot is pulling a calf out at three in the morning. I'd probably say it louder than I should, because Kofi in the parlour has been worried sick about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I get to keep learning my job without someone pulling the floor out. I'm still slow at the feeding sums and I lost a calf last winter because I didn't spot milk fever in its mother early enough. That still bothers me more than any computer does. If nothing changes, I've got time to get good at this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, mostly. I'd finish the calving and herd health course the co-op is paying for this spring, and I'd keep the savings where they are, not touch them. I'd also put my name forward again for the union branch committee, because the pay claim comes up in March and someone has to sit across from the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, I think. Steady. It's the first job I've had where I'm not counting the days to the weekend, so a world where it just carries on suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the calf you lost. What happened that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was February, minus four, and I saw the cow was down and thought she was just tired. Pete came in at six, took one look and said milk fever, but by then the calf she was carrying was gone. I went home and didn't eat. That's the job I want to get right, and a computer wouldn't have made me notice it any quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kofi, if AI really did stay this small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kofi to stop reading the stuff on his phone at night and get some sleep. Kofi's got three kids and he's frightened of a machine that hasn't turned up. I'd buy him a coffee and tell him the cows still need us both at five tomorrow.

say: AI is a **fancy search engine** and the bosses got excited over nothing.
No chatbot is going to **pull a calf** out at three in the morning.
think: I finally have **time to learn** this job properly without the floor moving under me.
My real worry is my own **skill gaps**, like missing milk fever and losing a calf last winter.
do: **Finish** the co-op's calving and herd health course this spring.
**Leave** the year of savings untouched and keep paying the mortgage as normal.
**Stand** for the union branch committee before the March pay claim.
feel: **Relieved** and steady, because this is the first job he doesn't count the days in.
S0.quote: No chatbot is pulling a calf out at three in the morning.
fieldNote: His biggest worry here is his own **inexperience**, not technology; the lost calf still weighs on him.
Strong **union pay deal** and nearly a year of savings make the plateau world feel secure.
Refuses the herd **phone app** and keeps a paper notebook, which shows how firmly he avoids new tools.

steps.text: Finish the co-op's calving and herd health course this spring
Stand for the union branch committee before the March pay claim

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office will feel it first, not us in the sheds. The ordering, the feed plans, the milk paperwork, that's what this card is talking about. I'd also say at the branch meeting that we need it in writing that nobody gets laid off because of a machine without retraining and notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the board has already had a salesman in about a robot milking unit. Pete told me in the parlour, quietly. If robots spread slowly, maybe it's ten years, maybe it's four, and I'm the newest stockman on the list. My job is fine today, but I've started noticing which cows walk into the parlour on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get the union to open talks on a technology agreement, so no job cuts without a year's notice and paid training. I'd add two hundred a month to the savings instead of the holiday fund. And I'd keep turning up and getting better, so if they pick who stays, it isn't an easy choice to drop me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit on edge, like hearing a noise downstairs at night. Nothing's happened, but I'm listening now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the salesman's visit look like from where you stood?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A man in a clean jacket walked through the shed pointing at the parlour, saying “eight stalls, two robots”. Nobody introduced him to us. The board chair was with him, and Kofi and I were scraping out and we just looked at each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office will feel it first. Who in the office do you think about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra does the milk records and the orders, she's been there twenty years. If software does the ordering and the planning, Sandra's job is half gone, and she's the one who sorted my payslip when it was wrong. I'd fight for Sandra the same as for the milkers.

say: The **office jobs** like ordering and feed plans feel this first, not the milkers in the sheds.
We need a **written agreement**: no lay-offs for machines without notice and paid retraining.
think: The board has already had a **robot milking** salesman in, and nobody told the staff.
As the **newest stockman**, I'd be first on the list if they cut milkers.
do: **Push** the union branch to open talks on a technology agreement.
**Move** two hundred a month from the holiday fund into savings.
**Keep improving** at the job so he isn't the easy one to drop.
feel: **On edge**, like hearing a noise downstairs at night.
Still **safe today**, but listening for change.
S1.quote: A man in a clean jacket walked through the shed pointing at the parlour, saying “eight stalls, two robots”. Nobody introduced him to us.
fieldNote: The **robot salesman** visit is a real event he keeps returning to.
He sees his own hands-on job as **safe for now**, but knows he's last in.
His first instinct is **collective**: a written deal, and he extends it to office staff like Sandra.

steps.text: Ask the union branch to open talks on a technology agreement
Move two hundred a month from the holiday fund to savings
Keep logging calvings and learning rations so he isn't easy to drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what unions are for, and anyone who laughed at paying dues should look again. I'd be on every group chat saying the government has to tax the robots and pay people while they're shut out. I wouldn't be quiet about it, and Amina would tell me to calm down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm finished at Brookfield by 2031. The thinking side goes first, so Pete's planning and Sandra's office are gone in 2028, and then three years later the robots come for the milking and the scraping, which is all I do. I'd be forty-eight, a former bus driver with two years on a farm, and buses won't need drivers either. Three years of warning sounds like a lot until you see what I'd be retraining into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop the holiday fund completely and throw every spare bit at the mortgage, so by 2031 there's less owing. I'd put my hand up to lead the union's campaign at the co-op, for a robot levy and a guaranteed wage while people move. And I'd go to every meeting and every protest about it, and vote on it, because it can't be every family for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. I lie awake working out the mortgage in my head, that kind of scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Idris and Leila?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Idris and Leila (his children) that Dad's job might go but we won't lose the house. Idris would ask what job to do, and I'd have no answer. We've got the savings, so it's not about food on the table. The question I couldn't answer is what would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never use AI tools. Would three years of warning change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amina asked me the same thing. Learning a computer to help the robot take my job, I can't see the sense in it. Maybe I'm being stubborn, but I'd rather spend those three years making sure the people who own the robots share what they make.

say: This is **what unions are for**, and anyone who laughed at paying dues should look again.
The government must **tax the robots** and pay people while they're shut out of work.
think: I expect to be **finished at Brookfield** by 2031, when robots do the milking and scraping.
The **three years** after thinking AI only buy time, because driving buses won't be an option either.
do: **Stop** the holiday fund and put every spare amount on the mortgage.
**Lead** the union's push for a robot levy and guaranteed wage at the co-op.
**Attend** every meeting and protest and vote for the levy.
feel: **Scared**, lying awake doing the mortgage sums in his head.
S2.quote: I'd tell Idris and Leila (his children) that Dad's job might go but we won't lose the house. Idris would ask what job to do, and I'd have no answer.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year gap** to fight collectively, not to retrain; he sees little worth retraining into.
Refuses AI tools even with warning: **stubbornness** he admits to himself.
The emotional peak is not money but having **no answer** for his son.

steps.text: Lead the union's robot levy and guaranteed wage campaign at Brookfield
Vote and march for a national robot tax
Overpay the Elmford mortgage with every spare amount
Stop the family holiday fund completely

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but with more time to organise. I'd say we have five years to get a deal in before the thinking machines and eight before the robots, so stop moaning and come to the branch meeting. I'd say it to the young lads especially, the ones who think it's not their problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd still lose the job, only in 2034 instead of 2031. I'd be fifty-one. The difference is that by then the mortgage could be mostly paid and Idris would be through school, so it's not the same cliff. It's a slower slope, but it's still the same slope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage hard, aiming to clear it by 2034 using the savings plus overpayments. I'd keep doing the union work and push the co-op to promise that the staff who stay get first go at the robot minding jobs. Beyond that, I wouldn't jump into anything yet; I'd wait and see which jobs are still standing in 2031 before I spent money on a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could sleep. There'd be a plan and a date on the fridge, and that makes a difference to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you be most glad to see gone by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, no question. If the house is ours, I can take a lower job, cleaning or whatever is left, and we'd still eat. My dad never owned a thing, and I'd like to be the first one who did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see before retraining. Isn't five years enough to learn something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to learn something, but learn what? Every course they'd offer me is a job the robots get in 2034 anyway. I'd rather watch for two or three years and then jump at something real.

say: We have **five years** before thinking AI and eight before the robots, so come to branch meetings.
The **young workers** need to see this is their problem too.
think: I'd probably still **lose the job**, just in 2034 at fifty-one instead of forty-eight.
With the **mortgage cleared** and kids grown, it's a slope rather than a cliff.
do: **Overpay** the mortgage to clear it by 2034.
**Push** the co-op to give current staff first pick of robot-minding jobs.
**Wait** until about 2031 before paying for any retraining course.
feel: **Worried but sleeping**, because there's a plan and a date on the fridge.
S3.quote: If the house is ours, I can take a lower job, cleaning or whatever is left, and we'd still eat.
fieldNote: The extra years turn panic into a **paid-off house** plan.
He still distrusts **retraining**, fearing any course leads to a job robots take too.
He'd use his union role to win **first pick** of new robot-minding work for current staff.

steps.text: Overpay the mortgage to clear it by 2034
Push Brookfield to give current staff first pick of robot-minding jobs
Hold off on paid courses until he sees which jobs survive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for the country to do it properly if they start now: training, a fund, a shorter working week. I'd say it on the union page and at the pub quiz, probably to people who are sick of hearing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2039 I'm fifty-six, the house is paid, Idris and Leila are grown. I'd still lose the milking job, I think, but that's a long way down the road. For the next few years nothing much touches me in the sheds, only the office side in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Brookfield and get properly good at the job, maybe herd manager when Pete retires. I'd keep paying into the union fund and push for an early pension deal for stock workers who lose out to robots. And I'd keep saving, nothing dramatic, just steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. It's still sad to think about the cows being milked by arms on rails, but it's not this year's problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss, if the robots did the milking in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss the quiet at five in the morning, when it's just me and the cows and the radio, more than the wage. Nobody's going to pay me for that bit, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your mind about AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If Pete's app was still there in ten years and still worked, I might let Leila show me how to use it. Don't write that down too loudly.

say: **Ten years** is enough for the country to plan training, a fund and shorter weeks.
Starting **right now** matters more than arguing about the exact date.
think: By 2039 he'd be **fifty-six**, with the house paid and the children grown.
For the **next few years** only the office side changes, not the sheds.
do: **Aim** for herd manager when Pete retires.
**Push** the union for an early pension deal for displaced stock workers.
**Keep saving** at the current steady rate.
feel: **Calmer**, though sad picturing cows milked by robot arms on rails.
S4.quote: I'd miss the quiet at five in the morning, when it's just me and the cows and the radio, more than the wage.
fieldNote: Long warning brings out **ambition**: herd manager, not just survival.
His loss is about **meaning** as much as money: the early quiet with the cows.
A rare crack in his resistance: he might let **his daughter** teach him the app.

steps.text: Work towards herd manager when Pete retires
Push the union for an early pension deal for stock workers
Keep saving at the same steady monthly amount

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Three years until robots in the parlour, and I'm the newest man there. What would help is a law that makes the owners share what the robots earn, a guaranteed wage while people move on, and a union strong enough to make it stick.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. If the co-op owns them, the farmers who own the co-op get richer and the workers get nothing. I'd want workers to own a share of every machine that takes a job.

headlineQuote: I'd want workers to own a share of every machine that takes a job.
portrait: Former **bus driver**, now a stockman two years into dairy work at a co-operative farm.
Strong **union pay** and a year of savings from his father's flat give him a real cushion.
Refuses **AI tools** and the herd app, and keeps a paper notebook in his pocket.
Calm in the plateau, **alarmed** at AGI by 2028 because robots could take the milking by 2031.
His answer to every scenario is **collective**: union deals, a robot levy and worker ownership.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots in the parlour by 2031 and him the newest stockman.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed wage** while people move, and a law making owners share robot earnings.
Workers owning a **share of machines** that take their jobs.
